title: The Order Record: Lifecycle, State and the Order Management System
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/13-order-management/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter. It is a contract, not a description: the places where the chapter did not yet do what the spec asks are listed under open_questions.

know: What an order record holds (header, lines, money, promises, goods, references) and why the order number is the key for creating the order in every other system.
The order's three status lines (money, goods per shipment, returns) and how the status the customer sees is computed from them.
Routing, split shipments and backorders, and what an order management system holds and what it leaves to the shop platform and the ERP.
believe: A single status word on an order hides facts that systems need, and is a fault, not a simplification.
The order's home is chosen by which system must answer the customer's question about a parcel.
can_do: Decide whether a merchant needs an OMS by checking four conditions.
Say what a split order's status should read and what the customer should be told.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or product manager who owns, or is about to own, an integration between the shop platform, a warehouse system and an ERP and must decide which system is the order's home. Service and operations managers get the vocabulary to ask why 'Delivered' was wrong.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 incidents in outline and the names of the sixteen failure patterns (meet-kestrel-and-pine, where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong).

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines of an order (money, goods, returns), 'system' as any software or outside service that takes part in handling an order, 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, the business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, and the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Part II: product, variant, SKU and GTIN; prices selected once at order placement and frozen; discounts allocated to lines; available-to-promise, one writer each for on hand and committed, per-channel buffers and an exact commit at checkout.

From the earlier chapters of Part III: checkout creates the order once, with its payment pending, keyed so that a retry does not create a second order; the payment provider's webhook marks it paid; authorization, capture, settlement and payout; one writing system and a business key for every action that moves money.
does_not_know: State machine; the order lifecycle, money, goods and return machines; fulfillment order; the order-level summary and its two rules.
Edit window, calculated order, hold, cancellation request, compensation and the saga pattern's vocabulary.
Sourcing, routing, split shipment, backorder, child shipment.
Orchestration; the OMS's components; the two-of-four rule.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a two-parcel order whose systems show three different statuses, the reader says what the order should have shown and which design decision was missing.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An order for a fleece and socks ships the fleece first; the socks wait for replenishment. The shop shows 'Delivered', the warehouse 'In picking' and the ERP 'Not invoiced'. Using only this chapter: what should the order have shown, and what was missing in its design?
acceptance_criteria.expected: 'Partially delivered: 1 of 2 parcels' (and 'ships in two parcels' to the customer): the goods status is held per shipment and the summary is taken from the least-advanced shipment. The design had one status word, so the first parcel's delivery marked the whole order delivered, and no one system held the order across the platform, the warehouse and the ERP.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a merchant's channels and locations, the reader decides whether it needs an OMS by the four conditions and says why an OMS rather than the ERP holds the order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant sells through its own web shop and a marketplace and ships from two warehouses. A vendor offers it an OMS. Using only this chapter: does it need an order hub, and should that hub be the ERP or an OMS?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Yes: two of the four conditions hold (several channels create orders; several locations fulfil them), so one system must be the order's home. An OMS rather than the ERP, because the hub must route lines between the warehouses and answer a customer's question about a parcel, which a finance system running in batches cannot. Not decided by revenue.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what happens when support cancels an order that has already shipped.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Support 'cancels' an order that has already shipped. Using only this chapter: what should happen instead?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A shipped order cannot be canceled; the cancellation becomes a return (return label, receipt, inspection, refund on receipt), a compensating step the order system coordinates. Edits lock once the warehouse has accepted the work.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why a single 'shipped' status misleads when the parts of an order move separately; what an order record holds; its separate states; routing and split shipments; where the order should live and when an OMS is needed. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Three-Status Order and its order-hub decision, platform and OMS vendor documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: Where does the order live once it is placed, what states does it pass through, and when does a merchant need an order management system (OMS)?
thesis.claim: Once placed, an order should live in one system that holds it as one record, under one order number, with three separate status lines (money: authorized, paid, refunded, moved by the payment provider's events; goods: requested, accepted, shipped, delivered, held per shipment and moved by the warehouse and the carrier; returns: requested, received, inspected, refunded or exchanged) and computes the status the customer sees from all its shipments, so that the order reads delivered only when every parcel has been delivered. While one channel creates orders and one location fulfils them, that system is the shop platform; a merchant needs an OMS as the order's home once at least two of four conditions hold (several channels create orders, several locations fulfil them, promises depend on the location, service agents cannot see one order across systems), because an OMS, unlike the ERP, can route lines between locations and answer a customer's question about a parcel.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that an order has one status in whichever system took it, kept in step with the others by connectors, and that an OMS is a product for large retailers, needed by revenue or order volume rather than by how many systems create and fulfil orders.
thesis.so_what: Order #1052877 read 'Delivered' in the platform, 'In picking' in the warehouse and 'Not invoiced' in the ERP while the customer had a fleece and no socks, and produced 11 support tickets; with goods status per shipment it would have read 'Partially delivered: 1 of 2 parcels'. Kestrel & Pine meets all four conditions, so under W2 it makes a bought OMS the order hub, with the platform keeping the checkout and the ERP the books. A merchant that accepts the claim counts its order sources and fulfilling locations and names the order's home before it buys anything.
thesis.how_why: Money, goods and returns are changed by different systems at different times (the payment provider, the warehouse and the carrier per parcel, the returns portal), so one status word lets the latest message overwrite the others: one parcel's delivery scan marked a two-parcel order delivered. Every system that copies the order receives it at least once, so the copies stay one order only through one number family with the order number as the key. With one channel and one location the platform's record sees every change; with several sources, each with its own connector to the warehouse and the books, no system sees the whole order; one condition alone can be handled by the platform plus a connector, but two make the joins between systems the problem, and choosing which location ships which line needs rules over stock, capacity, cut-off times and cost that the platforms' priority and distance rules do not hold. The ERP holds the financial record and runs in batches, so it cannot answer a parcel question.

supporting_claims.claim: An order record has six parts (header, lines, money, promises, goods, references), and its number, drawn from one family for every channel, is the key that lets every other system receive the 'order placed' message more than once and still hold one order.

Money, goods and returns are moved by different systems at different times, so the order keeps a separate state machine for each, the goods state lives on each shipment, and the status the customer sees is computed from the least-advanced shipment; one status word lets the latest message overwrite the others.

Edits, holds and cancellations are changes to those state machines, not form updates: edits close once the warehouse accepts the work, and a cancellation after shipment becomes a return, a compensating step the order's home coordinates.

Once several locations fulfil orders, choosing which location ships which line and whether to split is a cost decision over stock, capacity, cut-off times and carrier rates that the platforms' priority and distance rules do not make, and a split must be told to the customer.

The order's home is chosen by which system must answer the customer's question about a parcel: the shop platform while one channel creates orders and one location fulfils them, and an OMS, not the ERP, once two of four conditions hold, with the platform keeping the checkout and the ERP the books.

An order hub does not remove the joins between systems: messages are repeated, lost and reordered, so each join still needs the order or shipment id as its key, a state machine that refuses impossible moves and a daily comparison of the copies.

role.contribution: Gives the order one home and separate status lines, so that the payment outcome, each parcel and each return are kept without overwriting each other, and supplies the per-shipment record the ledger chapter invoices from.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene to states: the Three-Status Order, then the record and the state machines that answer it
choices, trade-offs and stages: four homes for the order on the same criteria, then by stage

flow.rationale: The Three-Status Order comes first so that every term arrives as part of the answer to 'why did three systems give three answers'. The record's parts and its number come before the state machines, because the machines are fields of that record and the number is the key every later section relies on. The state machines come before changes to a placed order, since an edit or a cancellation is a move of one of those machines, and before routing, since a split creates the second fulfillment order whose state the summary rule reads. Routing needs several locations, which the reader meets there for the first time, and ends on the fuller decision OMS vendors describe; the OMS as a product follows at once, so that it is known before the hub question is asked. Several channels then follow as the other half of the joins problem, with the two-of-four rule for when they need one home and three candidates for that home, the OMS among them; the choices weigh the four homes straight after the candidates, the built service joining them as the fourth announced there, with W2 named as the outcome of that comparison rather than its premise; the trade-off table compares them on the criteria the earlier sections set up plus time, cost and failure, and the stages place them by scale. The worked example shows the chosen design (W2) at work: its rollout, the requirements of each interaction once the OMS has been chosen (with an order like Eva's traced through it) and the replay of #1052877. The failures come last, opening from the repeated messages every design receives, because every design, the chosen one included, must expect them. Moving the scene later would put five sections of vocabulary before the problem; moving routing before the state machines would describe a split before the reader knows that the goods state belongs to each shipment; describing the OMS between the candidates table and the choices would interrupt the comparison; giving the OMS's requirements before the choice would assume a decision the chapter has not made.

hook.content: In December 2026 a Kestrel & Pine customer ordered a fleece and socks, and the fleece shipped first. The warehouse knew which item had left, the payment provider knew what was paid, and support had to explain when the socks would arrive, while the shop's status page said 'Delivered': one status word for an order whose parts moved separately misled both the customer and the team.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has received half an order has seen a status page that said more, or less, than the box held; the previous chapter has just marked Eva's order paid, and the opening's December 2026 order is the chapter's case.
bridge.to_topic: The facts about one order are known by different systems, so the question is which one record brings them together, how it keeps them apart, and which system holds it.

thesis_statement.text: An order needs one record that keeps money, goods per parcel and returns as separate status lines and computes the customer's status from all its parcels; the shop platform can hold it while one channel creates orders and one location fulfils them, and an order management system should hold it once two of four conditions hold, because it can route lines between locations and answer a parcel question.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Order #1052877
sections.controlling_idea: Order #1052877 showed three honest statuses in three systems because a partial shipment was collapsed into 'fulfilled' and the invoice waited for 'order complete', and nobody owned the combined view.

advances_thesis.how: Shows one status word overwritten by the latest message and no system holding the whole order, the two faults the thesis answers.

flow.rationale: The order, then what each system did as the days passed, then the tickets and the January review, then the decision; the decision makes sense only after the reader has seen that nobody owned the combined view.

transition_in.carries_over: The roadmap's first promise: the Three-Status Order.
transition_in.introduces: The order, its two items and what each system did.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Order #1052877, a €119 fleece and €18 socks, left Duiven in two parts: the fleece on 7 December, while the WMS kept the socks open as a second pick waiting for replenishment.

evidence.what: Order #1052877, €137, fleece shipped 7 December 2026, socks short in their pick location.
evidence.shows: The order became two shipments, the situation a single status cannot describe.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The agency's shipment-confirmation integration could not represent a partial shipment, so the first parcel marked the whole shop platform order fulfilled and its delivery on 8 December triggered 'Delivered': one confirmation, sent once and trusted (the Message in a Bottle).

transition_in.carries_over: The fleece shipped and the socks still open.
transition_in.introduces: What the integration did with the first shipment confirmation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Meanwhile the ERP waited for an 'order complete' message and showed 'Not invoiced', and the WMS showed 'In picking': each system exposed a different part of the situation.

evidence.what: Each system, what it held, its status and what the status was true of: the shop platform 'Delivered' (the first parcel), the WMS 'In picking' (the second pick), the ERP 'Not invoiced' (the invoice run), the customer 'Where are my socks?' (the order).

evidence.what: Figure 1: the customer's box without socks among three screens.

transition_in.carries_over: The shop platform's 'Delivered'.

transition_in.introduces: What it cost (eleven tickets) and the review's finding that nobody owned the order.

sections.heading: What an Order Record Holds
sections.controlling_idea: An order record has six parts that downstream systems read, is distinct from a cart, a shipment and an invoice, and carries one number from one family that every other system uses as the key for creating it.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the record the thesis says needs one home, and the number that keeps its copies one order.

flow.rationale: The whole record first, then the three things it is not, then the one field every system shares; the identity rules need the reader to know what is being identified.

transition_in.carries_over: W2's 'one home for every order'.
transition_in.introduces: What that home holds: the order record, part by part.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripped to what every downstream system needs, an order record has six parts: header, lines, money, promises, goods and references.

evidence.what: The six parts, what each holds and who reads it most.
evidence.shows: Each part has its own readers, so the record serves warehouse, finance, carrier, service and customer at once.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A cart is not an order, an order is not a shipment and an order is not an invoice.

transition_in.carries_over: The six parts of the record.
transition_in.introduces: Three neighbouring things it is often mistaken for.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The order number is shared by every system, the customer and the carrier label, so it comes from one family for every channel and is the idempotency key for creating the order anywhere else.

transition_in.carries_over: An order that may become several shipments and invoices.
transition_in.introduces: The one identifier that ties them together, and its two rules.

sections.heading: Several State Machines on One Record
sections.controlling_idea: An order carries separate state machines for its lifecycle, money, goods per shipment and returns, as the platforms' own documentation shows, and the status the customer sees is a summary computed from them under two rules.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the separate status lines in two vendors' models and gives the rule that makes a two-parcel order read 'partially delivered'.

flow.rationale: The term and the claim, then Shopify's and commercetools' models as evidence, then the summary rules that follow from them; the rules mean nothing before the reader knows the goods state lives on each shipment.

transition_in.carries_over: The record's money, goods and references parts.
transition_in.introduces: The states those parts move through, and that there are several.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A state machine is a fixed set of states and allowed moves; the Three-Status Order came from assuming an order has one, when it has at least three, the status lines named in Part I.
Shopify keeps three status families on one order: order, payment and fulfillment.

transition_in.carries_over: The claim that an order has several machines.
transition_in.introduces: The first platform's own model.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Below the order, each fulfillment order, the instruction to one location to ship a group of lines, has statuses of its own and a request status for the handshake with the warehouse.

evidence.what: Seven fulfillment-order statuses plus a request status.
evidence.shows: The goods state lives on each shipment, not on the order.

transition_in.carries_over: Shopify's statuses on the order.
transition_in.introduces: The statuses one level below, on each fulfillment order.

evidence.shows: A second vendor separates the same machines.

evidence.shows: The goods machine lives on each shipment and is moved by the warehouse and the carrier, not by the order system.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the goods state machine on each fulfillment order.

evidence.shows: The rule gives the answer the opening case lacked.

sections.heading: Changing a Placed Order
sections.controlling_idea: Edits, holds and cancellations are moves against the money, goods and stock commitments, governed by the goods state: edits close when the warehouse accepts the work, and a cancellation after shipment becomes a return.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that changing an order is a move of its state machines, and that the order's home coordinates the compensating steps.

flow.rationale: The general claim, then the three kinds of change in order of how far they reach: an edit changes work, a hold pauses it, a cancellation undoes it, and the last one defines compensation where it first needs it.

transition_in.carries_over: Separate machines, with the goods state on each shipment.
transition_in.introduces: What happens to them when a placed order is changed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Orders are edited, held or canceled more often than newcomers expect, and each change is a transaction against the money, goods and stock commitments, not a form update.

An edit changes work other systems may have accepted, so it is checked against the goods state and the amount paid, allowed only on unfulfilled lines, turned into a request once the warehouse has accepted the work, and sent to every system that holds a copy.

evidence.what: Shopify's calculated order, committed edit and unfulfilled-lines-only rule.
evidence.source: Shopify developer documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: A platform treats an edit as a validated transaction with a closing window.

transition_in.carries_over: Changes as transactions.
transition_in.introduces: The first kind: edits.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A hold stops fulfillment without canceling, and the stock stays committed while it waits.

evidence.what: Shopify: an order on hold keeps its inventory reserved.
evidence.shows: A hold pauses the goods machine without releasing the stock commitment.

transition_in.carries_over: Edits.
transition_in.introduces: The second kind: holds.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A cancellation before acceptance releases stock and voids or refunds the payment, but after shipment it becomes a return, a compensation that whichever system is the order's home coordinates.

evidence.what: The saga pattern's compensation vocabulary.
evidence.shows: Undoing a shipment is a later business step, not a rollback.

transition_in.carries_over: Holds.
transition_in.introduces: The third kind: cancellations, before and after shipment.

sections.heading: Routing, Sourcing and Splits
sections.controlling_idea: With more than one location, sourcing, routing and splitting become decisions over stock, capacity, cut-off times and cost that the platforms' simple rules do not make, and a split must be told to the customer.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the decision a single-location merchant never makes and that the platforms do not hold, one of the reasons an OMS becomes the home.

flow.rationale: The terms, then what the platforms decide and leave out, then what OMS vendors add, then the business trade-off in a split and its special case, the backorder; the vendors' fuller decision is read against the platforms' gaps.

transition_in.carries_over: The fulfillment order and the goods state per shipment.
transition_in.introduces: How an order becomes more than one fulfillment order when it can ship from several locations.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Once an order can be fulfilled from more than one location, three decisions appear: sourcing chooses the location for each line, routing is the rule set that makes the choice, and a split shipment is one order in several parcels.
Platforms route by simple rules over stock and geography, and do not know about capacity, cut-off times, carrier cost, marketplace fees or a maximum number of parcels.

evidence.what: Adobe Commerce source priority and distance priority; Shopify's assigned location, changeable only while the fulfillment order is open, scheduled or on hold.
evidence.source: Adobe Commerce documentation updated 2026-08-20; Shopify developer documentation, n.d.
evidence.shows: The platforms' routing is a priority list or the nearest location.

transition_in.carries_over: Routing as a rule set.
transition_in.introduces: The rules the platforms ship, and what they leave out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: OMS vendors describe the fuller decision: candidates and suggestions with reasons, child shipments for what is not in stock, splits that maximise items and minimise shipments under cost caps, and assignment to the location that keeps the promise most profitably.

evidence.what: Kibo's candidates, suggestions and child shipments; Fluent's split logic and caps; Manhattan's 'most profitably'.
evidence.source: Kibo, Fluent Commerce and Manhattan documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026
evidence.shows: The decision the platforms leave out has a documented shape that can be read as a specification.

evidence.shows: The same inputs decide whether to split now or wait.

transition_in.carries_over: What the platforms' rules do not know.
transition_in.introduces: What OMS vendors say the decision should take into account.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A split is a cost decision whose inputs are the carrier rates, the promise and the customer's channel, and whichever system makes it must also tell the customer 'two parcels'.

evidence.what: The fleece now and the socks later against one late parcel; the message nobody at Kestrel & Pine could send in December 2026.
evidence.shows: The trade-off and the missing message in the opening case.

transition_in.carries_over: The vendors' inputs to the split decision.
transition_in.introduces: The business trade-off inside one split and the message it requires.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A backorder is a split in time rather than space and needs the same honesty: a date from incoming stock and a message.

transition_in.carries_over: A split and the message it needs.

sections.heading: The OMS as a Product
sections.controlling_idea: An OMS takes every channel's orders, routes them, tracks them and gives service one view, and owns the operational order while leaving checkout and the books alone.

advances_thesis.how: Describes the system the thesis names as the home and its boundary with the platform and the ERP, before the hub question is asked.

flow.rationale: The product as vendors describe it, then its components and their boundaries; it follows routing because the fuller routing decision is one of its jobs, and it comes before the channels section so that the OMS is known when it is named as the third candidate for the order's home.

transition_in.introduces: The product those vendors sell: what an OMS does, component by component.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An OMS takes orders from every channel, decides which location fulfils each line, tracks each order through delivery and returns, and gives service one view; orchestration is its job of sequencing those steps, and the vendors describe the same shape.

sections.heading: Many Channels, One Record
sections.controlling_idea: When orders begin in several systems, each with its own connectors and vocabulary, one system must be the order hub once two of four conditions hold, and the question is which of three candidates owns which truth about the order.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the two-of-four rule for when the order needs a hub and frames the hub as a choice between the platform, the ERP and an OMS, each holding a different truth.

flow.rationale: The Spaghetti Junction first, then the rule for when it needs one record of its own, then the hub with its three candidates, then the boundary between them; the rule comes before the candidates because it decides whether a hub is needed at all, and the choice between candidates is left to the choices section.

transition_in.carries_over: Several locations, the routing decision and the OMS that can make it.
transition_in.introduces: Several channels creating orders, the other half of the joins problem.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Several channels creating orders are the other half of the joins problem: Kestrel & Pine's orders begin in four systems, each with its own connector to the warehouse, its own path to the books and its own status vocabulary, the Spaghetti Junction that adding one channel at a time produces.

evidence.what: Storefront and B2B portal orders in the shop platform, marketplace orders through the connector, EDI and 38% hand-keyed wholesale orders in the ERP, store sales as POS receipts.
evidence.shows: Four sources and four sets of connectors for one kind of record.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The junction needs one record of its own once at least two of four conditions hold (several locations, several channels, promises that depend on location, service that cannot see one order), because one can be handled by the platform plus a connector and two make the joins between systems the problem; Kestrel & Pine has had all four since 2023.

evidence.what: Figure 4: four condition cards, two ticked, leading to the order hub.
evidence.shows: The rule in one picture.

transition_in.carries_over: The Spaghetti Junction of four order sources.
transition_in.introduces: The rule for when that junction needs one record of its own.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The alternative to the junction is one order hub with one state model and one number family, and the real question is which of three candidates it should be (the platform, the ERP or the OMS just described), with building one's own left to the choices.

evidence.what: The platform, the ERP and an OMS: what each is good at, what it lacks, and at which stage it is common.
evidence.shows: Each candidate holds a different record well (customer-facing, financial, operational) and lacks what the others have.

transition_in.carries_over: The junction and the point at which it needs one record.
transition_in.introduces: One hub, and three candidates for it, with a fourth announced.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three records are three truths about the same order, so the decision is which system owns which truth and how the others are told.

evidence.what: Fluent Commerce: 'your ERP stays the system of record' for finance.
evidence.shows: An OMS vendor draws the same boundary between operational and financial records.

transition_in.carries_over: The three candidates and their strengths.
transition_in.introduces: That they are not rivals but owners of different truths.

sections.heading: The Choices
sections.controlling_idea: The order can live in the platform, the ERP, a bought OMS or a built service, and each fits a different merchant.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the four homes side by side, with W2 as the third.

flow.rationale: From the least to the most new software: the platform's own record, the ERP as hub, a bought OMS, a built service; each is described by what it covers, where it fits and what it costs.

transition_in.carries_over: The three candidates and the truth each owns.
transition_in.introduces: The four places the order can live, one by one, the fourth being a built service.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The platform's order can be the record, with apps and a WMS or 3PL connector around it; Shopify's features cover this well, and the absence of documented rule-based sourcing on cost, capacity or cut-off is its limit.
The ERP can be the order hub where wholesale dominates and the ERP partner is strong, at the cost of speed, a customer-facing state it cannot show and a hub owned by the finance system's vendor.

transition_in.carries_over: The platform as the record.
transition_in.introduces: The second option: the ERP.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A bought OMS as the hub is Kestrel & Pine's choice, W2 (the OMS holds every channel's order, the shop platform keeps the checkout and the storefront history, the ERP the financial record), priced as a third core system, its subscription and implementation, and the work of re-pointing every order source and the warehouse.

evidence.what: Illustratively €4,500 a month including the availability module, about €320,000 one-time implementation.
evidence.shows: The order of magnitude of the choice Kestrel & Pine made.

transition_in.carries_over: The ERP as hub.
transition_in.introduces: The third option, Kestrel & Pine's.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A built order service, the fourth option announced in the channels section, is right for a vendor whose product is commerce or a group with unusual rules, and wrong for a 14-person technology team, because the order record is where custom code is most expensive to get wrong.

transition_in.carries_over: A bought OMS.
transition_in.introduces: The fourth option: building one.

evidence.what: Four options against orders from every channel, state model, routing and splits, service view, time to value, running cost, exit cost and what breaks them.
evidence.shows: Only the bought OMS has one state model with separate machines, rule-based routing and one service screen; the platform breaks when a second channel or location arrives.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author would stay with the platform's order until two of the four conditions hold, then choose between the ERP and an OMS by asking who should answer a customer's parcel question, and build only when order management is the product.

transition_in.introduces: What the author would do.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: The record's shape is the same at every stage; what changes is how many systems create and fulfil orders, and the order needs a hub once two of the four conditions hold.

advances_thesis.how: Places the home decision on the scale stages and ties the change to the number of order sources and locations, not to revenue.

evidence.what: Four stages (Starting 2016-2018, Growing 2019-2022, Omnichannel 2023-, Group) with what is typical, what becomes necessary and the warning signs.
evidence.shows: The warning signs at each stage are joins between order copies, not volume.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An order has the same parts at every stage; what changes is how many systems create orders and how many fulfil them, and once two of the four conditions hold the order needs a hub.

transition_in.introduces: What stays the same across stages and what changes.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Order integrations fail in eight recurring ways, and most are recovered by an identity on every message, a state machine that refuses impossible moves and a daily comparison: a hub gives each join one key, one owner and one check.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the hub leaves the joins in place and says what each one needs.

transition_in.carries_over: The design working on the opening case.
transition_in.introduces: That the same design still receives repeated, lost and reordered messages, and the ways order integrations fail.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Even under the chosen design, order updates are messages, and repeating one must not repeat the order or shipment it describes, so the record must recognise a retry even when all systems work; the duplicate is one of eight ways order integrations fail.

evidence.what: Shopify's 13 billion webhooks for 2021 (2022-01-20), flagged as historical; Shopify warns an app may receive a webhook more than once.
evidence.source: Shopify Engineering, 2022-01-20; Shopify developer documentation, n.d.
evidence.shows: Duplicates are a property of the delivery mechanism, not a fault of a small merchant's systems.

evidence.what: Eight failures (duplicate order, lost confirmation, collapsed status, out-of-order events, edit after acceptance, cancel after shipment, routing nobody owns, stuck invoice trigger) with appearance, detection and recovery.
evidence.shows: The recoveries repeat: keys, state checks and reconciliation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Most failures end with the same recovery: an identity on every message, a state machine that refuses impossible moves and a daily comparison between the copies, so a hub gives each join one key, one owner and one check rather than removing it.

evidence.what: The recovery column of the failure table read across its rows.
evidence.shows: Most recoveries are a key, a state check or a daily comparison.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The opening's fleece-and-socks order, the separate state machines, the split and the hub question are one answer: each fact about an order is first known by a different witness (the payment provider, the warehouse per parcel, the carrier, the returns portal), so only one record that keeps each witness's line apart and is the one place every channel's order is created can say 'two parcels, one delivered'; which system holds it follows from who must answer that parcel question.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant can count its order sources and fulfilling locations against the four conditions, and write down the order's home, its number family and its per-shipment status, before any OMS is bought; Kestrel & Pine's remedy was that decision first and the purchase second.

callback.to: The opening's order, #1052877, whose fleece shipped before the socks while the status page said 'Delivered'.
callback.how: The first paragraph of the conclusion says what that order should read, who says it and which system holds it.

takeaway.content: Count the order sources and fulfilling locations against the four conditions, name the order's home and its number family, hold the goods state per shipment, and take the nine questions to your own company.

hand_off.introduces: The tax it carries, the invoice each shipment produces and the entries those documents post in the books.
